question_text: Find $k$ given the consecutive arithmetic terms:

mark_breakdown.desc: Set up common difference equation $k - 3 = 11 - k$

subparts.solution: If $3, k, 11$ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence, then $k - 3 = 11 - k$ {equating differences} $\therefore 2k = 14 \implies k = 7$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: In an arithmetic sequence, the difference between consecutive terms is constant: $u_2 - u_1 = u_3 - u_2$.

mark_breakdown.desc: Equate differences to form a quadratic equation

subparts.solution: If $-2, k + 4, k^2 + 11$ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence, then $k + 4 - (-2) = k^2 + 11 - (k + 4)$ {equating differences} $\therefore k + 6 = k^2 + 11 - k - 4 \implies k^2 - 2k + 1 = 0 \implies (k - 1)^2 = 0 \implies k = 1$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Consecutive terms have equal common differences: $u_2 - u_1 = u_3 - u_2$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Sign error when distributing the minus sign in $-(k+4)$.

mark_breakdown.desc: Equate differences to set up quadratic equation

subparts.solution: If $k - 5, 2k, 2k^2$ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence, then $2k - (k - 5) = 2k^2 - 2k$ {equating differences} $\therefore k + 5 = 2k^2 - 2k \implies 2k^2 - 3k - 5 = 0 \implies 2k^2 + 2k - 5k - 5 = 0 \implies 2k(k + 1) - 5(k + 1) = 0 \implies (k + 1)(2k - 5) = 0 \implies k = -1\text{ or } k = \frac{5}{2}$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Equate successive differences: $u_2 - u_1 = u_3 - u_2$ and solve the resulting quadratic equation.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Forgetting the negative root or making a sign error expanding $-(k-5)$.
